r: The Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses protect the right of same-sex couples to marry, and States must license and recognize those marriages.
f: Fourteen same-sex couples sued state officials in four States that defined marriage as one man and one woman or refused to recognize out-of-state same-sex marriages.
h: Bans struck down (5–4, Kennedy). Marriage is a fundamental right because it protects autonomy, supports an intimate union, safeguards children and families, and is a keystone of social order.
x: Background reading on courts recognizing unenumerated rights. Use it to discuss judicial review versus deference to legislatures (the Roberts dissent), not as Philippine law.
g: Read with Dobbs: the same Court later used a ‘history and tradition’ test to deny an unenumerated right. Expect a question on how courts choose between text, history, and evolving values.

r: The State may not use a public-accommodations law to compel a person to create expressive work (pure speech) conveying a message she disagrees with; the First Amendment bars compelled speech.
f: A web designer wanted to make wedding websites but not for same-sex weddings, and feared enforcement of Colorado’s anti-discrimination law.
h: Ruled for the designer (6–3, Gorsuch). Her custom websites are pure speech; Colorado cannot compel it. The Court also found a credible threat of enforcement, so the pre-enforcement suit was justiciable.
x: Shows a clash of two rights (equality versus speech) and a pre-enforcement challenge where standing rests on a credible threat. Compare with Philippine ripeness rules.
g: Paired with Obergefell to show the US Court narrowing the effect of an earlier rights ruling.

n: Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization
r: The Constitution confers no right to abortion; an unenumerated right is protected by due process only if deeply rooted in the Nation’s history and tradition and implicit in ordered liberty. Roe and Casey overruled.
f: Mississippi banned most abortions after 15 weeks; a clinic challenged it under Roe and Casey.
h: Law upheld; Roe and Casey overruled; abortion regulation returned to legislatures and reviewed only for a rational basis.
x: Use for stare decisis and when precedent may be overruled (quality of reasoning, workability, reliance). Useful in essays on constitutional change by courts.
g: Readings I are background for Gatmaytan’s theme that courts reshape constitutions. Keep it to one or two lines in an answer.

r: Constitutional provisions are presumed self-executing. A provision is self-executing if it is complete in itself, fixing the nature and extent of the right and the liability; Article II policies are generally not. Art. XII, Sec. 10(2) (Filipino First) is self-executing.
f: GSIS sold 51% of Manila Hotel through public bidding; a Malaysian firm outbid a Filipino corporation, which then matched the bid.
h: The Filipino bidder had to be preferred. The Manila Hotel is part of the national patrimony, and GSIS’s sale is State action.
x: Use when a law or official act ignores a constitutional command and the defense is ‘there is no enabling law yet.’ Answer: presumption of self-execution; the State cannot nullify a mandate by not legislating.
test: Self-executing if (1) complete in itself; (2) the nature and extent of the right are fixed; (3) the liability is fixed; (4) nothing refers the subject to Congress for action.

r: Under the 1935 Constitution, taxing a judge’s salary was a prohibited diminution of compensation; the guarantee protects judicial independence, not the judge personally.
f: Justice Perfecto paid ₱802 income tax on his 1946 salary and sued for a refund.
h: The refund was upheld. Taxing the salary diminished it.
x: A step in a historical line: Perfecto, then Endencia (Congress cannot overrule the Court by ‘interpreting’), then Nitafan (the 1987 framers intended salaries to be taxable).
w: The masterfile digest for this case has leftover template text (‘Hello, please copy paste’) in its application part. Rely on this card or the 2025 Reviewer.

r: Congress cannot interpret the Constitution by statute. A law declaring that taxing judges’ salaries ‘is not a diminution’ invades the judiciary’s exclusive power to interpret, and is void.
f: After Perfecto, Congress passed RA 590, Sec. 13, declaring that income tax on salaries is not a diminution of compensation, and taxed Justices Endencia and Jugo.
h: Sec. 13 of RA 590 was unconstitutional insofar as it applied to judges. Interpretation belongs to the courts.
x: Use whenever Congress tries to ‘define’ or ‘clarify’ a constitutional term or overturn a Supreme Court ruling by statute. Compare with Congress adding qualifications to constitutional offices.
g: Gatmaytan’s book cites Endencia for the core of separation of powers: the legislature makes laws but cannot interpret them, least of all the Constitution.

r: Judicial review extends to impeachment proceedings where the Constitution sets limits. ‘Initiate’ in Art. XI, Sec. 3(5) means the filing of the complaint and its referral to the Committee on Justice; a second complaint within one year is barred.
f: A first impeachment complaint against CJ Davide was dismissed; a day later, over one-third of House members filed a second complaint within the same year.
h: The second complaint was barred by the one-year rule; the House rules defining ‘initiation’ differently were unconstitutional.
x: Use for the three modes of interpretation (verba legis, ratio legis, ut magis valeat), for truly political versus justiciable questions, and for the one-year bar.
test: Political question if the Constitution commits the matter fully to a political branch with no limits; justiciable if the Constitution imposes limits (e.g., the one-year bar), which the Court must enforce.

n: In re Supreme Court Judicial Independence v. Judiciary Development Fund
r: The Court cannot rule on a bill: a bill is not a law, creates no rights, and its review would be an advisory opinion. Judicial review cannot be compelled by mandamus.
f: A citizen-taxpayer sought mandamus to stop Congress from passing bills abolishing the Judiciary Development Fund.
h: Dismissed: no actual case, no standing, and no ministerial duty to compel.
x: Use when the news is about a proposed bill or a pending Charter change resolution. The challenge is premature until the measure is enacted (see also Montesclaros).
g: Gatmaytan’s book treats this with Montesclaros under ‘When judicial review is not exercised.’

n: Nitafan v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue
r: Ratio legis est anima: the framers’ intent controls. The records of the Constitutional Commission show that judges’ salaries under the 1987 Constitution are subject to income tax; Perfecto and Endencia were discarded.
f: RTC judges sought to stop the withholding of income tax from their salaries, invoking the ‘shall not be decreased’ clause of Art. VIII, Sec. 10.
h: Petition dismissed; taxing judges’ salaries does not violate Art. VIII, Sec. 10.
x: Use to show how intent can override a literal reading; and that the Court, not Congress, settles constitutional meaning (contrast Endencia).

r: Constitutional provisions apply prospectively unless they provide otherwise. The 1987 rule that a waiver of counsel must be in writing and with counsel does not apply to confessions made under the 1973 Constitution.
f: A postal employee confessed in 1982 to a mail-van robbery after waiving counsel without a lawyer, then invoked the 1987 rule.
x: Use when a new constitutional or charter provision is applied to acts done before it took effect.

n: J.M. Tuason & Co. v. Land Tenure Administration
r: Verba legis: words of the Constitution take their ordinary meaning unless technical terms are used; the Constitution is not a lawyer’s document. Read with its purpose of social justice.
f: RA 2616 authorized the expropriation of the Tatalon Estate in Quezon City for resale to its occupants.
h: RA 2616 was upheld as within Congress’s express power to expropriate landed estates for resale; the equal protection challenge failed.
x: Cite for the plain-meaning rule. The masterfile has two digests (Decision and Resolution).

r: Art. XVII, Sec. 2 (people’s initiative) is not self-executing: it needs an implementing law. RA 6735 is inadequate for initiatives to amend the Constitution, and COMELEC cannot fill the gap by resolution.
f: The Delfin petition sought to lift term limits through a people’s initiative, filed with COMELEC before gathering signatures.
h: COMELEC was barred from acting on the Delfin petition, and its resolution on initiative procedure was voided.
x: Any People’s Initiative story: ask (1) is there an adequate enabling law; (2) is it an amendment or a revision (Lambino); (3) did the people author and sign the petition.
g: Gatmaytan’s book walks through the three reasons RA 6735 was found inadequate (Sec. 2 silence, no petition contents, no subtitle). Know them.

r: Whether Congress, acting as a constituent assembly, followed the Constitution is justiciable, not political. Amendments may be submitted at a plebiscite held with a general election (proper submission doctrine).
f: Congress proposed amendments (more House seats; allowing members to sit in a convention) and a law set the plebiscite with the 1967 elections.
h: The law was upheld; simultaneous plebiscite is not unconstitutional.
x: Use when Congress proposes Charter change: its acts as a constituent assembly can be reviewed; the date of the plebiscite may coincide with an election if the people can still be informed.

r: Doctrine of proper submission: all amendments proposed by the same Convention must be submitted together, so the people have a full frame of reference. No piecemeal submission.
f: The 1971 Convention scheduled a plebiscite on a single amendment (lowering the voting age to 18) ahead of its other proposals.
h: The advance plebiscite was enjoined as unauthorized.
x: Use when proponents of Charter change propose one ‘test’ amendment first, or a ‘piecemeal’ plebiscite.

r: The validity of a presidential decree calling a plebiscite to ratify a proposed Constitution is a justiciable question.
f: Marcos, under martial law, issued PD 73 calling a plebiscite on the 1973 Constitution, then replaced it with Citizens’ Assemblies.
h: Dismissed as moot when the plebiscite was postponed; the main opinion nonetheless held the issue justiciable.
x: Read as the prelude to Javellana.

r: Six Justices held the 1973 Constitution was not validly ratified under Art. XV of the 1935 Constitution, but the petitions were dismissed (6–4), leaving ‘no further judicial obstacle’ to the new Constitution being considered in force.
f: Marcos proclaimed the 1973 Constitution ratified through Citizens’ Assemblies (show of hands, voters as young as 15, under martial law) instead of a COMELEC plebiscite.
h: Votes: 6 held the issue justiciable; 6 held it was not validly ratified; on acceptance by the people, 4 said yes, 2 (Concepcion, Zaldivar) said no free acceptance was possible under martial law, and 4 said they could not tell; 6 voted to dismiss the petitions.
x: Use for: political question doctrine; ratification needs a real plebiscite; ‘acquiescence’ as a non-legal basis for a Constitution; and the duty of courts under authoritarian rule.
g: His favorite case. Gatmaytan: the Court ‘looked the other way,’ removed itself from institutional significance, and lost public respect. Read Concepcion (justiciable; not ratified; no proof of acquiescence), Zaldivar (same; votes under martial law cannot show free acceptance), and Makasiar (political question; the people accepted it).

r: A people’s initiative may only propose amendments, not revisions. The people must author and sign the entire proposal, and it must be embodied in a petition shown to them when they sign.
f: The Lambino group gathered 6.3 million signatures to shift to a unicameral parliamentary system, but the signature sheets did not contain the full text.
h: Petition dismissed (8–7): the signature sheet is not the petition; and the proposal is a revision under both the quantitative and qualitative tests.
x: Use for any initiative or Charter change story: amendment or revision; who authored it; whether the text was shown to signatories.
test: Revision or amendment: (1) quantitative test — is the change so extensive that it alters the substantial entirety of the Constitution? (2) qualitative test — does it alter the basic plan of government (e.g., presidential to parliamentary, bicameral to unicameral)?
g: Gatmaytan (‘Changing Constitutions’): the Court redeemed itself after Javellana; the campaign was government-driven, not a true people’s initiative.
